Youth are at the heart of Korea’s transition to 100% renewable energy

“Serving Up Renewable Energy,” a youth talk concert on climate action, concludes successfully.

GEYK proposes “Neo-vestment,” a new approach to investment beyond divestment.

On Saturday, September 28, GEYK held “Serving Up Renewable Energy” on the second floor of KB Youth Maru. The talk concert was supported by the global climate NGO 350.org.

The youth event was part of an annual project run by GEYK and 350.org since 2014. It gives young people a leading role in responding to climate change and moving toward 100% renewable energy.

Experts from international organizations and civil society joined young participants to share Korean and international examples of withdrawing investment from coal, phasing out coal power, and shifting to renewables. The presentations led to lively discussion and networking. GEYK proposed “Neo-vestment,” a new approach to deciding where capital should go in an era of climate change.

The expert panel included Lim Dae-woong, the Korea representative of the UN Environment Programme Finance Initiative (UNEP FI); Lee So-young, a lawyer and deputy director of Solutions for Our Climate; and Yoo Jong-jin, secretary-general of the Dangjin Federation for Environmental Movement. GEYK members Cho Gyu-ri, Kim Ji-min, and Yoon Sang-ho joined as youth panelists and moderator.

In the first presentation, GEYK representative Cho Gyu-ri shared her experience working on coal divestment and finance with Asian youth at a 350.org climate leadership camp. She described visiting a coal plant in Southeast Asia and seeing how untreated smoke and wastewater threatened nearby Indigenous residents’ health, livelihoods, and homes. She explained why a shift from coal to renewable energy is also a matter of climate justice.

Lee So-young explained that coal-fired power produces the most greenhouse gas emissions of any electricity source, and that under the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C scenario, coal plants would have to close by 2040. She noted that nine Korean public financial institutions had invested around 23 trillion won in coal power. KDB, the only Korean implementing entity for the Green Climate Fund, was still investing in plants at home and overseas. While leading international institutions were leaving coal because of project-finance risks, she argued that Korea was moving in the opposite direction.

UNEP FI’s Lim Dae-woong described sustainable and climate finance as an opportunity to manage climate risks and channel capital toward new investments. He explained that growing awareness of climate change’s effect on the real economy was moving finance from an ESG focus toward the Sustainable Development Goals, the Principles for Responsible Banking, and new rules on disclosure. He highlighted the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), which asks firms to assess financial risks in their portfolios under different climate scenarios and disclose them. UNEP FI was piloting the approach. He warned that if those rules were implemented strongly, financial institutions that ignored the development goals could face substantial provisions and liabilities, lower profits, and weaker finances.

Yoo Jong-jin explained why South Chungcheong Province, the first Korean province to introduce a coal-free treasury designation policy, needed to act urgently. Thirty of Korea’s 60 coal-fired units were operating in the province, and three of the world’s five largest coal power stations were in Taean, Dangjin, and Boryeong. In July, the province added criteria to compare and score financial institutions on their coal phaseout commitments and coal investments when selecting its treasury bank. Yoo emphasized cooperation between civil society and government to expand the policy nationwide.

After the panel, the audience and speakers exchanged ideas during a Q&A and networking session. The discussion showed how young people could think together about divestment, phasing out coal, and the transition to 100% renewable energy.
